text: On 2 November 2012 the Ankara Assize Court decided to suspend the execution of the sentence imposed on Filiz Uluçelebi under section 7(2) of Law no. 3713 (Prevention of Terrorism Act), in accordance with provisional section 1 of Law no. 6352.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The suspension of the sentences of Levent Çakır, Serdar Kır, Selçuk Mart and Filiz Uluçelebi was for a period of three years, on condition that they did not commit an offence when expressing ideas and opinions through the medium of the press or other media, or by any other means.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: On 1 April 2005 Law no. 5237 (the Turkish Criminal Code) entered into force.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: At the material time, Article 220 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that anyone who establishes or directs an organisation for the purpose of criminal activity shall be liable to a term of imprisonment of between two and six years, provided that the structure of the organisation, the number of members and the quantity of equipment and supplies are sufficient to commit the intended crimes.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: At the material time, Article 220 § 2 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that anyone who becomes a member of an organisation established for the purpose of criminal activity shall be liable to a term of imprisonment of between one and three years.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: At the material time, Article 220 § 3 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that if the organisation is armed, the sentences stated in Article 220 §§ 1 and 2 shall be increased by between one quarter and one half.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: At the material time, Article 220 § 4 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that any crime committed within the framework of the organisation's activities shall be punished separately.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: At the material time, Article 220 § 5 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that the heads of a criminal organisation shall also be sentenced as perpetrators of all crimes committed within the framework of the organisation's activities.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: At the material time, Article 220 § 6 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that anyone who commits a crime on behalf of an illegal organisation, even if he is not a member of that organisation, shall also be punished for being a member of the organisation.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: At the material time, Article 220 § 7 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that anyone who aids an illegal organisation knowingly and willingly, even if he does not belong to the hierarchical structure of the organisation, shall be punished as a member of the organisation.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: At the material time, Article 220 § 8 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that anyone who spreads propaganda for the organisation or its objectives shall be punished by a term of imprisonment of between one and three years, and if the crime is committed through the press or other media, the sentence shall be increased by one half.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Paragraphs 6 and 7 of Article 220 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) were amended by Law no. 6352, which entered into force on 2 July 2012.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: As amended by Law no. 6352, Article 220 § 6 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provides that anyone who commits a crime on behalf of an illegal organisation, even if he is not a member of that organisation, shall also be punished for being a member of the organisation, and the penalty to be imposed for membership may be reduced by up to half.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: As amended by Law no. 6352, Article 220 § 7 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provides that anyone who aids an illegal organisation knowingly and willingly, even if he does not belong to the hierarchical structure of the organisation, shall be punished as a member of the organisation, and the penalty to be imposed for membership may be reduced by up to two thirds, depending on the nature of the assistance.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Article 314 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provides that anyone who forms an armed organisation to commit the crimes listed in the fourth and fifth sections of the relevant chapter, or commands such an organisation, shall be liable to a term of imprisonment of between ten and fifteen years.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Article 314 § 2 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provides that anyone who becomes a member of an armed organisation mentioned in Article 314 § 1 shall be liable to a term of imprisonment of between five and ten years.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Article 314 § 3 of the Turkish Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provides that other provisions relating to the crime of establishing an organisation for the purpose of criminal activity are also applicable to the crime of membership of an armed organisation under Article 314.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Between 7 August 2003 and 18 July 2006, section 7(2) of Law no. 3713 (Prevention of Terrorism Act) provided that any person who assists members of terrorist organisations or who disseminates propaganda inciting others to violence or other methods of terrorism shall be liable to a term of imprisonment of one to five years and a judicial fine of five million liras to one billion liras.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE
B. Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713)

text: The first sentence of section 7(2) of Law no. 3713 (Prevention of Terrorism Act) was amended by Law no. 5532, which entered into force on 18 July 2006, to read: 'Any person who disseminates propaganda in favour of a terrorist organisation shall be liable to a term of imprisonment of one to five years.'
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE
B. Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713)

text: The first sentence of section 7(2) of Law no. 3713 (Prevention of Terrorism Act) was amended on 30 April 2013 by Law no. 6459 to read: 'Any person who disseminates propaganda in favour of a terrorist organisation by justifying, praising or encouraging the use of methods constituting coercion, violence or threats shall be liable to a term of imprisonment of one to five years.'
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE
B. Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713)

text: At its 106th plenary session, held on 11 and 12 March 2016, the Venice Commission (European Commission for Democracy through Law) adopted an Opinion on Articles 216, 299, 301 and 314 of the Penal Code of Turkey (CDL-AD(2016)002).
section_path: A. European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission noted that the Turkish Penal Code does not contain a definition of an armed organisation or an armed group.
section_path: A. European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: In its judgment E. 2006/10-253 K. 2007/80 of 3 April 2007, the General Criminal Board of the Court of Cassation of Turkey listed the main criteria that a criminal organisation for the purposes of Article 220 of the Turkish Penal Code should display, including: the group must have at least three members; there must be a tight or loose hierarchical connection between members; an 'abstract link' between members is not sufficient; members must have a common intention to commit crimes; the group must present continuity in time; and the structure, number of members, tools and equipment must be sufficient for the commission of the envisaged crimes.
section_path: A. European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission noted that the Court of Cassation of Turkey developed the criterion of 'membership' in an armed organisation by examining different acts of the suspect, taking account of their 'continuity, diversity and intensity' in order to determine whether those acts prove an 'organic relationship' with the organisation or whether the acts may be considered as committed knowingly and wilfully within the 'hierarchical structure' of the organisation.
section_path: A. European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission noted that if an 'organic relationship' with the organisation cannot be proven on the basis of acts attributed to the defendant which do not present any 'continuity, diversity or intensity', the paragraphs on 'aiding and abetting an armed organisation' or 'committing crime on behalf of an armed organisation' under Article 220 of the Turkish Penal Code may be applied.
section_path: A. European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission noted that according to non-governmental sources, in the application of Article 314 of the Turkish Penal Code, domestic courts in many cases decide on the membership of a person in an armed organisation on the basis of very weak evidence, raising questions as to the 'foreseeability' of the application of Article 314.
section_path: A. European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: Amnesty International, in its 2013 Report on Turkey, considered that conduct which is not in itself criminal, such as activity related to the exercise of the rights to freedom of assembly, association and expression, is considered as evidence of membership of defendants in an armed organisation by Turkish courts.
section_path: A. European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: Amnesty International's 2013 Report on Turkey stated that individuals have been prosecuted for membership of a terrorist organisation on charges relating solely to their engagement in peaceful and, in themselves, lawful pro-Kurdish activities.
section_path: A. European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission noted that in the case of Yılmaz and Kılıç v. Turkey (application no. 68514/01), the European Court of Human Rights considered that where the only evidence which led to the criminal conviction of the applicants under Article 169 of the former Turkish Penal Code was forms of expression (statements by the applicants, content of the slogans they shouted during a public demonstration), it should be concluded that there was an interference with the applicants' right to freedom of expression.
section_path: A. European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission noted that the European Court of Human Rights applied the same principle in the case of Gül and Others v. Turkey (application no. 4870/02) and held that the criminal conviction of the applicants on the basis of Article 169 of the former Turkish Penal Code constituted an interference with their right to freedom of expression, since the only evidence used against them was the content of the slogans they shouted during a public demonstration.
section_path: A. European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission stated that conviction on the basis of weak evidence in the application of Article 314 of the Turkish Penal Code may create problems in the field of Article 7 of the Convention, since that provision embodies the principle that the criminal law must not be extensively construed to an accused's detriment, for instance by analogy.
section_path: A. European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission stated that any allegation of membership of an armed organisation must be established with convincing evidence and beyond any reasonable doubt.
section_path: A. European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission recommended that the established criteria in the case law of the Court of Cassation of Turkey — that acts attributed to a defendant should show 'in their continuity, diversity and intensity' an 'organic relationship' to an organisation, or prove that the defendant acted knowingly and willingly within the 'hierarchical structure' of the organisation — should be applied strictly.
section_path: A. European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission stated that the expression of an opinion in its different forms should not be the only evidence before domestic courts to decide on the membership of a defendant in an armed organisation.
section_path: A. European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission noted that paragraph 3 of Article 314 of the Turkish Penal Code provides that all other provisions related to the crime of establishing an organization to commit a crime will be applied in conjunction with Article 314.
section_path: A. European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission noted that in many recent judgments of the Court of Cassation of Turkey, Article 314 of the Turkish Penal Code was applied in conjunction with paragraphs 6 and 7 of Article 220, on the basis of the reference made in Article 314(3) to 'other provisions' related to forming a criminal organisation.
section_path: A. European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission noted that in a judgment of 4 March 2008, the General Criminal Board of the Court of Cassation of Turkey held that acts such as participating in a public demonstration following a general call from pro-PKK media outlets, making a victory sign and shouting slogans to support the leader of a terrorist organisation, and clashing with the security forces, are considered crimes committed on behalf of the terrorist organisation, and that the defendant was convicted as a member of a criminal organisation under Article 220 § 6 applied in conjunction with Article 314 of the Turkish Penal Code, although membership in an armed organisation was not established.
section_path: A. European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission noted that in a judgment of 24 March 2011, the 9th Chamber of the Court of Cassation of Turkey held that participation in an illegal public demonstration following a general call of an armed organisation on its Internet site, covering one's face during a demonstration, and shouting slogans in support of the armed organisation were considered as committing crimes on behalf of an armed organisation, and the defendant was convicted as a member of an armed organisation under Article 220(6) in conjunction with Article 314 of the Turkish Penal Code, although his membership was not proven.
section_path: A. European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission noted that Article 220(7) of the Turkish Penal Code, concerning aiding and abetting an organisation knowingly and willingly, was applied in the Nedim Şener case, where the applicant was prosecuted under Article 314(3) in conjunction with Article 220(7) for having contributed, at the request of suspected members of a criminal organisation, to the preparation of books criticising the actions of the government.
section_path: A. European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission noted that in a judgment of 4 June 2012 of the Court of Cassation of Turkey, the preparation of a declaration stating 'If it is a crime to refer to Öcalan as Mr. Öcalan, I hereby commit this crime and I denounce myself' and the collection of signatures for this declaration, in the framework of a campaign instigated by a terrorist organisation on its internet sites, was considered as 'knowingly and willingly aiding the criminal organisation'.
section_path: A. European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission noted that a new paragraph was added to Article 7 of the Anti-Terror Law no. 3713 by an amendment of 11 April 2013, providing that those who committed the crime of propaganda in support of a terrorist organisation under Article 7(2), the crime under Article 6(2) of printing and disseminating declarations by terrorist organisations, or the crime under Article 28(1) of the Public Demonstrations Law no. 2911 of participating in an unlawful demonstration, shall not be sentenced separately under Article 220(6) of the Turkish Penal Code.
section_path: A. European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission welcomed the amendment introduced to Article 7 of the Anti-Terror Law no. 3713, which excluded the above-mentioned crimes from the scope of application of Article 220(6) of the Turkish Penal Code.
section_path: A. European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission considered that the scope of the amendment to Article 7 of the Anti-Terror Law no. 3713 is rather limited and does not provide for sufficient protection to the exercise of freedom of expression and assembly, in particular because the amendment excluded the mentioned crimes only from the scope of Article 220(6) but not from Article 220(7) of the Turkish Penal Code.
section_path: A. European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission recommended that the sentence 'although he is not a member of that organisation, shall also be sentenced for the offence of being a member of that organisation' in paragraphs 6 and 7 of Article 220 of the Turkish Penal Code be repealed.
section_path: A. European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: In its Opinion CDL-AD(2016)002, the Venice Commission recommended that, should the sentence in paragraphs 6 and 7 of Article 220 of the Turkish Penal Code be maintained, the Turkish authorities should consider limiting the application of Article 220 in conjunction with Article 314 to cases which do not involve the exercise of the rights to freedom of expression and assembly.
section_path: A. European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission)

text: In a report published on 10 January 2012 (CommDH(2012)2), Mr Thomas Hammarberg, the former Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe, reported on a visit to Turkey between 10 and 14 October 2011.
section_path: B. Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe

text: Mr Thomas Hammarberg stated in his report of 10 January 2012 that any allegation of terrorist activity must be established with convincing evidence and beyond any reasonable doubt.
section_path: B. Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe

text: Mr Thomas Hammarberg stated in his report of 10 January 2012 that violence or the threat to use violence is an essential component of an act of terrorism, and that restrictions of human rights in the fight against terrorism must be defined as precisely as possible and be necessary and proportionate to the aim pursued.
section_path: B. Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe

text: Mr Thomas Hammarberg stated in his report of 10 January 2012 that the provisions contained in the Turkish anti-terror legislation and Article 220 of the Turkish Criminal Code allow for a very wide margin of appreciation, in particular in cases where membership in a terrorist organisation has not been proven and when an act or statement may be deemed to coincide with the aims or instructions of a terrorist organisation.
section_path: B. Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe

text: Mr Thomas Hammarberg encouraged the Turkish authorities in his report of 10 January 2012 to reflect on and address concerns about the wide margin of appreciation in Turkish anti-terror legislation and Article 220 of the Turkish Criminal Code through legislative measures and/or case-law.
section_path: B. Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe

text: In a memorandum on freedom of expression and media freedom in Turkey (CommDH(2017)5), published on 15 February 2017, Mr Nils Muižnieks, the Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe, reported on a visit to Turkey between 6 and 14 April 2016.
section_path: B. Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe

text: Mr Nils Muižnieks, in his memorandum CommDH(2017)5 of 15 February 2017, stressed the need for a complete overhaul of the Turkish Criminal Code, including Article 220 §§ 6 and 7 and Article 314.
section_path: B. Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe

text: Mr Nils Muižnieks, in his memorandum CommDH(2017)5 of 15 February 2017, considered that the overhaul of the Turkish Criminal Code should take full account of the European Court of Human Rights' case-law and the opinion of the Venice Commission (CDL-AD(2016)002).
section_path: B. Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe

text: On 1 November 2010 Human Rights Watch published a report entitled 'Protesting as a Terrorist Offence / The Arbitrary Use of Terrorism Laws to Prosecute and Incarcerate Demonstrators in Turkey'.
section_path: 1. Report of Human Rights Watch of 1 November 2010

text: The Human Rights Watch report of 1 November 2010 was seventy-five pages long and mainly concerned trials and convictions of demonstrators in Turkey under Laws nos. 5237, 2911 and 3713.
section_path: 1. Report of Human Rights Watch of 1 November 2010

text: The Human Rights Watch report of 1 November 2010 stated that many hundreds of people in Turkey face prosecution, or are serving substantial sentences for terrorism convictions, where their 'crime' was to engage in peaceful protest, or to throw stones or burn a tire at a protest.
section_path: 1. Report of Human Rights Watch of 1 November 2010

text: The Human Rights Watch report of 1 November 2010 stated that legal amendments since 2005, along with case law since 2008, have allowed courts in Turkey to convict demonstrators under the harshest terrorism laws, by invoking two articles of the Turkish Penal Code in combination with the Anti-Terror Law.
section_path: 1. Report of Human Rights Watch of 1 November 2010

text: The Human Rights Watch report of 1 November 2010 stated that Article 220 of the Turkish Penal Code (Law no. 5237) has been most commonly used to punish criminal gangs, but courts have also applied it to those deemed to be associated with armed political organizations.
section_path: 1. Report of Human Rights Watch of 1 November 2010

text: The Human Rights Watch report of 1 November 2010 stated that Article 220/7 of the Turkish Penal Code has in some cases been applied to leftist demonstrators who have been punished as 'members' of armed organizations for 'knowingly and willingly aiding' them without providing any material assistance.
section_path: 1. Report of Human Rights Watch of 1 November 2010

text: The Human Rights Watch report of 1 November 2010 stated that Turkish Penal Code Articles 220/6 and 220/7 are so vaguely worded and lacking in clarity about what is prohibited as to offer an individual no indication of how to regulate or limit conduct.
section_path: 1. Report of Human Rights Watch of 1 November 2010

text: The Human Rights Watch report of 1 November 2010 recommended that the Turkish Government urgently amend Turkish Penal Code Article 220 and repeal Articles 220/6 and 220/7, which are vague, lack legal clarity and specificity, and are therefore subject to arbitrary application.
section_path: 1. Report of Human Rights Watch of 1 November 2010

text: The Human Rights Watch report of 1 November 2010 recommended that a review board be set up to examine all cases concluded under Articles 220/6 and 220/7 of the Turkish Penal Code for compliance with international human rights law obligations, with a view to quashing sentences under Turkish Penal Code Articles 314/2 and 314/3 in connection with Articles 220/6 and 220/7.
section_path: 1. Report of Human Rights Watch of 1 November 2010

text: On 27 March 2013 Amnesty International published a report entitled 'Turkey: Decriminalize Dissent / Time to deliver on the Right to Freedom of Expression'.
section_path: 2. Report of Amnesty International of 27 March 2013

text: The Amnesty International report of 27 March 2013 stated that Article 220/7 of the Turkish Penal Code criminalises assisting a terrorist organisation and is a self-standing offence that does not require the commission of a further criminal act.
section_path: 2. Report of Amnesty International of 27 March 2013

text: The Amnesty International report of 27 March 2013 stated that Article 220/7 of the Turkish Penal Code allows for the sentencing of those convicted under it as though they were members of the organisation they are found to have assisted.
section_path: 2. Report of Amnesty International of 27 March 2013

text: The Amnesty International report of 27 March 2013 stated that Article 220/7 of the Turkish Penal Code is often used to prosecute conduct protected by the rights to freedom of expression, association and assembly.
section_path: 2. Report of Amnesty International of 27 March 2013

text: The Amnesty International report of 27 March 2013 stated that the choice of prosecutors to prosecute under Article 220/6 or Article 220/7 of the Turkish Penal Code often appears arbitrary, with similar behaviour sometimes prosecuted under one, sometimes under the other, and sometimes under Article 314 directly.
section_path: 2. Report of Amnesty International of 27 March 2013

text: The Amnesty International report of 27 March 2013 stated that when prosecutors seek to convict a person under Article 220/7 of the Turkish Penal Code, they often do not provide evidence demonstrating a link to a terrorist organisation, nor do they attempt to prove that the accused was engaged in any criminal offence or in aiding and abetting, other than supposedly assisting the proscribed organisation.
section_path: 2. Report of Amnesty International of 27 March 2013

text: The Amnesty International report of 27 March 2013 stated that no inference should be drawn from someone undertaking a lawful act, such as participating in a peaceful demonstration, even if such acts benefit, through lawful means, goals shared by a terrorist organisation.
section_path: 2. Report of Amnesty International of 27 March 2013

text: The Amnesty International report of 27 March 2013 urged the Turkish government to adopt guidelines for prosecutors on the application of Article 220/7 of the Turkish Penal Code that set out clear criteria for when assisting an armed group can be criminalized, including the requirement that such assistance must either in and of itself be a recognizable criminal offence, or be directly linked to the planning or commission of one.
section_path: 2. Report of Amnesty International of 27 March 2013
